content: Brine is a solution of water that is either saturated or nearly saturated with sodium chloride (NaCl). Historically, it has been widely used for preserving vegetables, fish, and meat, although its popularity for this purpose has declined over time. It remains commonly employed in the aging process of cheeses such as Halloumi and Feta. Brine functions as a preservation agent in a manner similar to sugar or vinegar, but it also has significant applications in heat transportation. The addition of salt to water lowers the freezing point of the solution, enhancing its efficiency as a heat transfer medium at a relatively low cost. Brine is frequently used to pre-treat roadways in preparation for winter storms. When applied to roads alongside salt pellets, it lowers the freezing point of surface water, facilitating the melting of snow and ice at higher temperatures, thereby improving road safety. In ice rinks, such as those used for hockey or skating, brine is cycled through refrigeration systems and returned beneath the ice slab at a colder temperature to maintain the ice surface. It is also utilized in the cooling systems of cruise vessels and as a quenching medium for cooling ferrous metals. In Europe, brine baths are sometimes employed medicinally to treat various conditions, including skin disorders and bladder issues. In the offshore oil and gas industry, brine mixed with monoethylene glycol (MEG) is used to flood pipelines before commissioning to prevent hydrate formation during production startup. This application depends on the specific properties of the well. In Arctic regions, brine is used in underground mining to enable water-fed drills to operate without freezing in permafrost conditions. Additionally, chilled brine is employed for localized freezing of water to allow mine shafts to be sunk without the risk of flooding. Brine is commonly used in the drying of organic solvents following an aqueous wash. The brine wash removes the majority of water from the organic solvent, with any remaining water typically removed using chemical methods, such as anhydrous magnesium sulfate. In industrial processes, brine is electrolyzed in the chlor-alkali process to produce sodium hydroxide, chlorine, and hydrogen, as well as hypochlorite and chlorate salts. During this process, chloride ions are oxidized to chlorine gas, while water is reduced to hydrogen gas and hydroxide ions. The hydroxide ions combine with sodium ions to form sodium hydroxide upon evaporation. By adjusting the reaction conditions, the chlorine gas can also react with hydroxide ions to produce hypochlorite and chlorate ions. Brine is also integral to the Solvay process for producing sodium carbonate and is used in solution mining to extract salt from underground deposits. In the pharmaceutical industry, brines are employed for various applications. When used industrially, brine is typically transported through pipelines made of welded steel, which are coated to protect against corrosion.
